title: Active Scanning
summary: Active scanning is the reconnaissance category where the adversary sends traffic directly to victim infrastructure instead of reading third party sources, accepting that the traffic may be logged in exchange for fresher and more certain results. The family includes sweeping address ranges for live hosts, probing services for software and version detail, and enumerating content through brute force requests. Because every packet reaches the target, this is the most detectable reconnaissance tactic available to a defender, and it is also the noisiest. Adversaries manage the noise by slowing the scan over hours or days, distributing it across many source addresses, and mixing probes into ordinary looking web requests, so a simple rate threshold will not catch everything. The valuable defender artefacts are firewall and netflow records, web access logs, intrusion detection alerts and honeypot hits, correlated by source, timing and port coverage. What separates hostile scanning from legitimate activity, such as vulnerability management scanners, search engine crawlers and health checks, is authorisation and change control rather than the packet shape itself.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker sends network traffic to your systems to see what answers. They are testing doors, not opening them. The aim is to learn which computers are online and which services they offer.
beginner.whyItMatters: Active scanning is usually the step just before an attack. If you notice it early, you get a warning and time to react. It also creates noise on your network, which means you can detect it. Ignoring it means you lose your best chance to prepare.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a range of internet addresses that belong to your organisation.
They send simple test messages, such as ping requests, to see which addresses answer.
They probe common service ports on the addresses that replied, one after another.
They read the responses for details such as software names and version numbers.
They often repeat the scan slowly over many hours, or from many addresses, to look less obvious.
They write down the reachable systems and services and plan which one to attack.
beginner.example: Think of a person walking along a street at night and gently tapping each door to hear which ones sound hollow. They do not enter any house. They simply build a list of which homes are occupied and which doors are weak, then return later to the one they chose.
takeaways: Active scanning touches your network, so it can always be logged and alerted on.
Slow, spread out scans beat simple rate limits, so correlate across sources.
Keep an approved scanner list so you can tell sanctioned tests from hostile probing.

objectives: Define active scanning and contrast it with passive reconnaissance.
List the common scan types and the information each one produces.
Identify the telemetry sources that record scanning against your perimeter.
Explain evasion methods adversaries use and how correlation defeats them.
Describe how to whitelist and schedule authorised vulnerability scanning.
